title: Chapter 8: Income, Expenditure, and the Keynesian Cross
benchmark: Paul Krugman & Robin Wells, Macroeconomics (Principles SSOT, Spring 2027)

questions.title: Defining Disposable Income
questions.prompt_template: In the aggregate consumption function C = C_0 + cY_D, what does disposable income (Y_D) measure?

hints.text: Think about the exact algebraic expression Y_D = Y - T used in the consumption function.
Remember that T denotes net taxes—taxes collected by the government minus transfer payments sent to households.

options_template.text: Total household income retained after subtracting net taxes (taxes minus government transfer payments).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Disposable income is defined as Y_D = Y - T, where T represents net taxes (taxes paid minus government transfers received), measuring the income households actually have available to spend or save.

options_template.text: Total national income before any taxes or government transfer payments are accounted for.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Gross vs. Disposable Income): Total pre-tax income is Y, not Y_D; households cannot spend income collected as net taxes.

options_template.text: Household income left over after subtracting both net taxes and all consumption spending.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Saving Confused with Disposable Income): Subtracting consumption from disposable income yields private saving (S = Y_D - C), not disposable income.

options_template.text: Only the portion of household income earned from wages, excluding transfer payments and capital income.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wage-Only Misconception): Disposable income includes all after-tax household income plus government transfers, not solely labor wages.

questions.title: Meaning of Autonomous Consumption
questions.prompt_template: What does autonomous consumption (C_0 > 0) represent in the aggregate consumption function?

hints.text: Evaluate the consumption function C = C_0 + cY_D when current disposable income Y_D equals zero.
Ask how households pay for basic necessities like food and shelter if their current income temporarily drops to zero.

options_template.text: The fraction of each additional dollar of disposable income that households spend on consumer goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept vs. Slope Confusion): The fraction of an additional dollar spent is the marginal propensity to consume (MPC), which is the slope rather than the intercept C_0.

options_template.text: Baseline household spending on necessities that occurs even if current disposable income is zero, financed by drawing down past savings or borrowing.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Autonomous consumption C_0 is the income-independent component of consumer spending—baseline outlays for food, shelter, and utilities financed through dis-saving or borrowing when Y_D = 0.

options_template.text: Government spending on public goods and infrastructure that does not depend on real GDP.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Consumption vs. Government Purchases): Government outlays are denoted by G, whereas C_0 is strictly the autonomous component of household consumption.

options_template.text: Total household saving that occurs automatically when disposable income equals the break-even level.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Break-Even Confusion): At the break-even level of disposable income, household saving is zero (S = 0), whereas C_0 is positive baseline spending at Y_D = 0.

questions.title: Why MPC and MPS Sum to One
questions.prompt_template: Why must the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) and the marginal propensity to save (MPS) always sum to 1?

hints.text: Consider the two exhaustive uses of an extra dollar of after-tax disposable income.
Start from the accounting identity Delta Y_D = Delta C + Delta S and divide both sides by Delta Y_D.

options_template.text: Because autonomous consumption C_0 always equals autonomous saving -C_0 in equilibrium.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Autonomous vs. Marginal Confusion): The identity MPC + MPS = 1 governs how an incremental dollar of disposable income is divided, not the level of autonomous intercepts.

options_template.text: Because total consumption always equals total disposable income across all income levels.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Saving Fallacy): Consumption equals disposable income only at the break-even point; at other income levels households either save or dis-save.

options_template.text: Because every additional dollar of disposable income must be either spent on consumption or saved (Delta Y_D = Delta C + Delta S).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Dividing the identity Delta Y_D = Delta C + Delta S by Delta Y_D gives 1 = (Delta C / Delta Y_D) + (Delta S / Delta Y_D) = MPC + MPS.

options_template.text: Because the government sets net taxes equal to the difference between MPC and MPS.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Leakage Confusion): Net taxes are already subtracted before computing disposable income Y_D, so the MPC + MPS = 1 identity applies strictly to after-tax disposable income.

questions.title: Determinants of Planned Investment
questions.prompt_template: In the baseline Keynesian cross model, why is planned investment spending (I_planned) treated as exogenous (autonomous) rather than a linear function of current disposable income?

hints.text: Contrast what motivates households to buy groceries with what motivates firms to build factories or buy machinery.
Recall the three primary drivers of I_planned highlighted in Section 2: expected future profitability, capacity utilization, and the real interest rate.

options_template.text: Because planned investment consists exclusively of unintended warehouse inventory buildups.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Planned vs. Unplanned Investment Confusion): Unintended warehouse buildups are unplanned inventory investment (I_unplanned), whereas I_planned reflects firms' intended capital and inventory purchases.

options_template.text: Because planned investment depends primarily on expected future profitability, capacity utilization, and the real interest rate rather than current disposable income.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Firms' intended purchases of machinery, commercial structures, software, and planned inventory additions are driven mainly by forward-looking profitability, capacity utilization, and real interest rates, so the baseline model treats I_planned as autonomous.

options_template.text: Because planned investment is legally fixed by Congress each fiscal year alongside government purchases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Private vs. Public Spending Confusion): Planned investment is undertaken by private firms, not set by Congressional appropriations.

options_template.text: Because planned investment is always zero in short-run macroeconomic equilibrium.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Investment Fallacy): In short-run equilibrium, unplanned inventory investment (I_unplanned) is zero, while planned investment (I_planned) is typically positive.

questions.title: Accounting Identity for Unplanned Inventories
questions.prompt_template: Which equation correctly expresses the relationship between actual real GDP (Y), planned aggregate expenditure (AE_planned), and unplanned inventory investment (I_unplanned)?

hints.text: Start from the national accounting identity Y = C + I + G + NX and split actual investment I into planned and unplanned components.
Substitute I = I_planned + I_unplanned and group C + I_planned + G + NX into AE_planned, then solve for I_unplanned.

options_template.text: I_unplanned = Y - AE_planned, because actual investment equals I_planned + I_unplanned.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since actual output Y = C + I_planned + I_unplanned + G + NX = AE_planned + I_unplanned, rearranging gives I_unplanned = Y - AE_planned.

options_template.text: I_unplanned = AE_planned - Y, because unsold goods reduce actual GDP below planned spending.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal Error): When output Y exceeds planned sales AE_planned, unsold goods pile up, making I_unplanned positive (Y - AE_planned > 0), not negative.

options_template.text: I_unplanned = Y + AE_planned, because inventories are counted twice in national income accounts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Counting Fallacy): Unplanned inventory change is the gap between output and planned spending, not their sum.

options_template.text: I_unplanned = I_planned - S_private, because unplanned inventories exist only when households dis-save.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Saving-Investment Misidentification): Unplanned inventory changes reflect the gap between total output Y and total planned spending AE_planned, not merely I_planned minus private saving.

questions.title: Condition for Short-Run Macroeconomic Equilibrium
questions.prompt_template: Short-run macroeconomic equilibrium (Y*) in the Keynesian cross occurs exclusively when which pair of conditions holds?

hints.text: Ask what must be true for firms to have no reason to raise or lower their production levels.
Recall the adjustment law I_unplanned = Y - AE_planned: equilibrium requires zero unintended inventory accumulation or depletion.

options_template.text: Household saving equals zero (S_private = 0) and the government budget is balanced (G = T).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Break-Even and Balanced-Budget Fallacy): Short-run equilibrium does not require zero household saving or a balanced budget; it requires total output to equal total planned spending.

options_template.text: Actual real GDP equals planned aggregate expenditure (Y = AE_planned) and unplanned inventory investment equals zero (I_unplanned = 0).
options_template.feedback: Correct. When Y = AE_planned, firms sell exactly what they planned to sell, so I_unplanned = Y - AE_planned = 0 and firms have no incentive to expand or cut production.

options_template.text: Planned investment equals zero (I_planned = 0) and consumption equals disposable income (C = Y_D).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Planned-Investment Fallacy): Planned investment is normally positive in equilibrium; only unplanned inventory investment must be zero.

options_template.text: Actual output exceeds planned aggregate expenditure (Y > AE_planned) so firms maintain a positive inventory buffer.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Disequilibrium Accumulation Fallacy): Whenever Y > AE_planned, unplanned inventories accumulate (I_unplanned > 0), prompting firms to cut production until Y falls to Y*.

questions.title: Why Firms Adjust Output Rather Than Prices in the Short Run
questions.prompt_template: In the Keynesian cross model, why do firms respond to a sudden dip in weekly sales primarily by adjusting production quantities and inventories rather than immediately slashing prices?

hints.text: Think about the short-run rigidities that prevent firms from repricing goods and wages every week.
Recall the three microeconomic frictions cited in Section 3: menu costs, multi-quarter wage contracts, and sticky catalog prices.

options_template.text: Because menu costs, multi-quarter wage contracts, and sticky catalog prices make immediate price cuts costly in the short run.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Short-run nominal rigidities—such as menu costs, multi-quarter wage contracts, and sticky catalog prices—cause firms to hold prices fixed temporarily and adjust output quantities and buffer inventories instead.

options_template.text: Because the Keynesian cross assumes the economy is always operating at full employment with flexible prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Long-Run Classical Confusion): Flexible prices and full employment characterize the long-run classical benchmark, not the short-run fixed-price Keynesian cross.

options_template.text: Because federal law prohibits retail firms from discounting merchandise during economic downturns.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Regulatory Myth): Price stickiness in the Keynesian model stems from economic frictions like menu costs and contracts, not legal prohibitions.

options_template.text: Because cutting prices automatically reduces planned aggregate expenditure by lowering autonomous consumption C_0.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Consumption Direction Confusion): Lower prices actually raise real purchasing power rather than reducing C_0; the Keynesian cross holds prices fixed due to short-run stickiness.

questions.title: Understanding the Paradox of Thrift
questions.prompt_template: What does John Maynard Keynes's 'paradox of thrift' describe in a recessionary economy with sticky prices?

hints.text: Distinguish what happens when one household saves more versus when every household cuts spending at the same time.
Recall S = -C_0 + sY_D: a drop in C_0 shifts the saving line up, but the resulting fall in Y reduces induced saving.

options_template.text: Higher individual saving always leads to higher equilibrium GDP because banks immediately lend every saved dollar.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Say's Law / Loanable-Funds Confusion): In a sticky-price recessionary Keynesian cross, an autonomous cut in consumption reduces aggregate expenditure and output rather than automatically raising investment.

options_template.text: When the government runs a budget surplus, households automatically reduce their marginal propensity to save to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fiscal-Household Confusion): The paradox of thrift concerns a simultaneous increase in desired household saving (a drop in C_0), not a government surplus forcing MPS to zero.

options_template.text: If all households simultaneously try to save more by cutting autonomous consumption (C_0), aggregate expenditure and national income fall, which can leave aggregate saving unchanged or even lower.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because private saving depends on income (S = -C_0 + sY_D), a collective drop in C_0 shrinks AE_planned and equilibrium income Y, offsetting the intended rise in aggregate saving.

options_template.text: Households that save more during a boom cause hyperinflation by driving up the autonomous spending multiplier.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Saving-Multiplier Sign Error): Higher saving (a higher MPS) lowers the multiplier rather than raising it, and does not cause hyperinflation.

questions.title: Economic Mechanism Behind the Spending Multiplier
questions.prompt_template: Why does a $1 increase in autonomous government purchases (Delta G = +$1) raise short-run equilibrium real GDP by more than $1 in the baseline Keynesian cross?

hints.text: Trace what happens to the dollars paid to transit workers and suppliers in Round 1 when they spend those earnings in Round 2.
Think about the infinite geometric series Delta A_0 (1 + c + c^2 + c^3 + ...) generated by induced consumption.

options_template.text: Because the initial spending becomes income for workers and suppliers, who then spend a fraction (MPC) of that income, triggering successive rounds of induced consumption.
options_template.feedback: Correct. One person's spending becomes another person's income, creating an infinite geometric series of induced consumption rounds (1 + c + c^2 + ... = 1 / (1 - c)).

options_template.text: Because higher government purchases automatically raise the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) above 1.0.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MPC > 1 Fallacy): In the Keynesian cross, MPC is held constant strictly between 0 and 1; the multiplier exceeds 1 even with a fixed MPC < 1.

options_template.text: Because firms double their planned investment spending whenever government purchases increase.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Endogenous Investment Assumption): In the baseline Keynesian cross, I_planned is held exogenous; the amplification comes from induced household consumption.

options_template.text: Because the government finances the purchase by printing money that directly lowers lump-sum taxes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monetary-Fiscal Conflation): The autonomous spending multiplier operates purely through income-induced consumption rounds in the expenditure stream, independent of money creation or tax cuts.

questions.title: Why the Tax Multiplier Is Smaller in Magnitude Than the Spending Multiplier
questions.prompt_template: In the baseline closed economy with lump-sum taxes, why is the absolute value of the lump-sum tax multiplier (|k_T|) always smaller than the autonomous spending multiplier (k_G)?

hints.text: Compare the Round 1 increase in planned aggregate expenditure from Delta G = +$1 versus Delta T = -$1.
Compare k_G = 1 / (1 - c) with |k_T| = c / (1 - c) and notice what happens to the saved fraction (1 - c) in Round 1.

options_template.text: Because lump-sum tax cuts reduce disposable income in Round 1, causing households to cut spending.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Error on Tax Cuts): A lump-sum tax cut (Delta T < 0) raises disposable income Y_D = Y - T rather than reducing it.

options_template.text: Because a $1 government purchase enters aggregate expenditure immediately at 100% of its value, whereas households save a fraction (MPS) of a $1 tax cut in Round 1 and spend only MPC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Direct purchases raise Round 1 spending by $1, while a $1 tax cut raises Round 1 consumption by only MPC (< $1) because households save MPS of the rebate immediately.

options_template.text: Because lump-sum taxes are subject to import leakages whereas government purchases never leak into imports.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Open-Economy Leakage Misattribution): Even in a closed economy with zero imports (m = 0), |k_T| = c/(1-c) is still strictly smaller than k_G = 1/(1-c) by exactly 1.

options_template.text: Because tax cuts change the slope of the AE_planned line whereas government purchases only shift its intercept.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Lump-Sum vs. Proportional Tax Confusion): Lump-sum taxes T do not change the slope c of AE_planned; they shift the vertical intercept by -c Delta T.

questions.title: The Balanced-Budget Multiplier Theorem
questions.prompt_template: In the baseline closed economy with lump-sum taxes, if the government increases purchases by Delta G and simultaneously raises lump-sum taxes by the exact same amount (Delta T = Delta G), what happens to short-run equilibrium GDP?

hints.text: Add the autonomous spending multiplier k_G = 1/(1 - c) and the lump-sum tax multiplier k_T = -c/(1 - c).
Notice that 1/(1 - c) + (-c)/(1 - c) simplifies to (1 - c)/(1 - c) regardless of the value of c in (0, 1).

options_template.text: Equilibrium GDP does not change (Delta Y* = 0) because the contractionary tax hike completely cancels the expansionary spending increase.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Symmetric Cancellation Fallacy): Because k_G = 1/(1-c) is larger in magnitude than k_T = -c/(1-c), the two effects do not cancel; their sum is 1, not 0.

options_template.text: Equilibrium GDP falls by Delta G because higher taxes permanently lower the marginal propensity to consume.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Contractionary Direction Error): Higher lump-sum taxes do not alter MPC, and the direct +Delta G injection outweighs the -c Delta T consumption drop.

options_template.text: Equilibrium GDP rises by exactly Delta G, because the balanced-budget multiplier equals k_BB = k_G + k_T = 1.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Adding the two multipliers yields k_BB = 1/(1 - c) - c/(1 - c) = (1 - c)/(1 - c) = 1, so Delta Y* = 1 x Delta G = Delta G.

options_template.text: Equilibrium GDP rises by k_G x Delta G because lump-sum taxes have no effect on planned aggregate expenditure.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Tax Drag): Raising lump-sum taxes reduces disposable income and consumption by c Delta T in Round 1, which offsets part—but not all—of the spending multiplier.

questions.title: Defining Automatic Stabilizers
questions.prompt_template: Which feature best defines an 'automatic stabilizer' in the macroeconomic expenditure model?

hints.text: Focus on the word 'automatic'—does it require a new vote by Congress?
Recall the U.S. examples in Section 5: progressive income taxes, corporate profit taxes, and Unemployment Insurance.

options_template.text: A discretionary Congressional stimulus bill passed quickly after a recession begins.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Discretionary vs. Automatic Confusion): Discretionary fiscal policy requires new legislation from Congress, whereas automatic stabilizers operate without new legislative action.

options_template.text: A central bank rule that fixes the nominal interest rate at zero during all phases of the business cycle.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monetary vs. Fiscal Stabilizer Confusion): Automatic stabilizers are built-in fiscal features of the tax and transfer system, not a permanent zero-interest-rate policy.

options_template.text: Built-in fiscal mechanisms—such as proportional income taxes and Unemployment Insurance—that automatically cushion disposable income and output swings without requiring new legislation.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When output falls in a recession, proportional tax liabilities automatically decline and Unemployment Insurance outlays automatically rise, dampening the downturn without legislative delay.

options_template.text: A balanced-budget constitutional amendment requiring Congress to cut spending whenever tax revenues fall.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pro-Cyclical Destabilizer Confusion): Cutting government spending during a recession amplifies rather than stabilizes output swings.

questions.title: Income-Sensitive Leakages in an Open Economy
questions.prompt_template: In an open economy with proportional income taxes (T = T_0 + tY) and induced imports (IM = IM_0 + mY), what are the three income-sensitive leakages that siphon purchasing power out of each domestic spending round?

hints.text: Look at the slope of the open-economy expenditure line: c(1 - t) - m.
Identify every channel through which an extra dollar of national income Y fails to become spending on domestically produced goods.

options_template.text: Private saving, proportional income taxes, and induced imports.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Out of each additional dollar of national income Y, households pay t in taxes, save (1 - c)(1 - t) of after-tax income, and spend m on foreign imports—leaving c(1 - t) - m for induced domestic spending.

options_template.text: Autonomous consumption, planned investment, and exports.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Injections Confused with Leakages): C_0, I_planned, and EX_0 are autonomous injections into domestic expenditure, not income-sensitive leakages.

options_template.text: Government purchases, transfer payments, and unplanned inventory depletion.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Injections vs. Leakages Confusion): Government purchases and transfers add to spending rather than leaking out of the domestic circular flow.

options_template.text: Menu costs, sticky catalog prices, and multi-quarter wage contracts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Nominal Rigidities vs. Leakages Confusion): Nominal rigidities explain why prices are sticky in the short run, not why purchasing power leaks out of spending rounds.

questions.title: Intercept and Slope of the Consumption Function
questions.prompt_template: On a graph with disposable income (Y_D) on the horizontal axis and aggregate consumption (C) on the vertical axis, what do the vertical intercept and slope of the consumption line C = C_0 + cY_D represent?

hints.text: Match C = C_0 + cY_D to the standard slope-intercept form y = b + mx.
Recall Figure 1: the consumption line starts above the origin at C_0 and is flatter than the 45-degree line.

options_template.text: The vertical intercept is autonomous consumption (C_0) and the slope is the marginal propensity to consume (c = MPC < 1).
options_template.feedback: Correct. When Y_D = 0, C = C_0 (the vertical intercept); for each $1 increase in Y_D, consumption rises by Delta C / Delta Y_D = c = MPC, which is positive but flatter than the 45-degree line.

options_template.text: The vertical intercept is the break-even income level and the slope is the marginal propensity to save (MPS).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Consumption vs. Saving Slope Confusion): The slope of the consumption line is MPC, not MPS (MPS is the slope of the saving schedule), and break-even income occurs at the 45-degree intersection.

options_template.text: The vertical intercept is zero and the slope is 1.0, matching the 45-degree reference line.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (45-Degree Line Confusion): A line through the origin with slope 1 is the 45-degree reference line (C = Y_D), not the consumption function.

options_template.text: The vertical intercept is net taxes (T) and the slope is the autonomous spending multiplier (k_G).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplier-Slope Confusion): The consumption line plots C against Y_D with intercept C_0 and slope c < 1, not intercept T or slope k_G > 1.

questions.title: Identifying Saving and Dis-Saving Regions
questions.prompt_template: On the aggregate consumption diagram containing both the consumption line (C = C_0 + cY_D) and the 45-degree reference line (C = Y_D), how are household saving and dis-saving represented?

hints.text: Remember that along the 45-degree line, vertical height equals horizontal distance (C = Y_D).
Compare the vertical height of C to the vertical height of the 45-degree line (Y_D) to determine the sign of S = Y_D - C.

options_template.text: To the left of the intersection, the consumption line lies above the 45-degree line (C > Y_D), indicating dis-saving (S < 0); to the right, it lies below the 45-degree line (Y_D > C), indicating positive saving (S > 0).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since S = Y_D - C, whenever C is vertically above the 45-degree line (left of break-even), households dis-save (S < 0); to the right of break-even, C lies below the 45-degree line and saving is positive (S > 0).

options_template.text: To the left of the intersection, households have positive saving (S > 0); to the right of the intersection, households dis-save (S < 0).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Region Reversal Error): Because the consumption line starts above the origin and has slope c < 1, C > Y_D at low incomes (left) and C < Y_D at high incomes (right).

options_template.text: At the intersection with the 45-degree line, household saving reaches its maximum positive value.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Break-Even Misinterpretation): At the 45-degree intersection, C = Y_D, so private saving is exactly zero (S = 0).

options_template.text: Household saving is always zero everywhere along the consumption line because C_0 offsets induced saving.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Saving Everywhere Fallacy): Saving equals zero only at the single break-even income level where C = Y_D.

questions.title: Movement Along vs. Shift of the Consumption Function
questions.prompt_template: On a graph of the aggregate consumption function C = C_0 + cY_D, what distinguishes an increase in current disposable income (Y_D) from an increase in autonomous consumption (C_0)?

hints.text: Check which variable is plotted on the horizontal axis of the consumption diagram.
In y = b + mx, changing x moves along the line, whereas changing the intercept b shifts the line vertically.

options_template.text: Both cause a parallel upward shift of the consumption function.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-Only Fallacy): Changing the variable on the horizontal axis (Y_D) moves the economy along the existing curve rather than shifting it.

options_template.text: An increase in Y_D causes a movement upward along the existing consumption line, whereas an increase in C_0 shifts the entire consumption line vertically upward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because Y_D is plotted on the horizontal axis, changes in Y_D produce movements along C = C_0 + cY_D, while changes in the vertical intercept C_0 shift the entire line upward in parallel.

options_template.text: An increase in Y_D rotates the consumption line steeper, whereas an increase in C_0 causes a movement along the line.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Rotation-Movement Confusion): Changing Y_D does not alter the slope c, and changing C_0 shifts the vertical intercept rather than moving along the old line.

options_template.text: An increase in Y_D shifts the 45-degree reference line to the right, whereas an increase in C_0 flattens the consumption line.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (45-Degree Line Shift Fallacy): The 45-degree line is a fixed geometric reference (C = Y_D) that never shifts.

questions.title: Role of the 45-Degree Line in the Keynesian Cross
questions.prompt_template: In the 45-degree Keynesian cross diagram with real GDP (Y) on the horizontal axis and planned aggregate expenditure (AE_planned) on the vertical axis, what does the 45-degree line represent?

hints.text: Consider what is true about the vertical and horizontal coordinates at every point on a 45-degree line through the origin.
At a 45-degree angle (slope = 1), the vertical value (AE_planned) equals the horizontal value (Y).

options_template.text: The economy's consumption function when autonomous consumption equals zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Consumption-Line Confusion): Even if C_0 = 0, the consumption function has slope c < 1, whereas the 45-degree line has slope 1.

options_template.text: The locus of all points where planned aggregate expenditure equals actual real GDP (AE_planned = Y), so unplanned inventory investment is zero.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Every point on the 45-degree line satisfies AE_planned = Y, making it the geometric equilibrium reference line where I_unplanned = 0.

options_template.text: The maximum productive capacity (potential GDP) of the economy in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (LRAS Confusion): Potential GDP is a vertical reference level of Y, not a 45-degree line.

options_template.text: The government's balanced-budget constraint showing all combinations where G = T.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fiscal-Constraint Confusion): The 45-degree line equates total planned expenditure to total output, not government spending to taxes.

questions.title: Interpreting Output Below Equilibrium (Y < Y*)
questions.prompt_template: On the Keynesian cross diagram, suppose current real GDP (Y) lies to the left of the equilibrium intersection E* (so Y < Y*). What does the vertical gap between the AE_planned line and the 45-degree line indicate?

hints.text: Check which line is vertically higher to the left of the intersection point E*.
When AE_planned > Y, evaluate the sign of I_unplanned = Y - AE_planned and ask how firms respond to emptying shelves.

options_template.text: AE_planned exceeds Y, causing unplanned inventory depletion (I_unplanned < 0) and prompting firms to expand production toward Y*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. To the left of E*, the AE_planned line lies above the 45-degree line (AE_planned > Y). Shelves empty faster than anticipated (I_unplanned < 0), motivating firms to hire workers and raise output.

options_template.text: Y exceeds AE_planned, causing unplanned inventory accumulation (I_unplanned > 0) and prompting firms to cut production.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Left-Right Region Reversal): Because AE_planned has slope less than 1, it lies above—not below—the 45-degree line to the left of E*.

options_template.text: AE_planned exceeds Y, causing unplanned inventory accumulation (I_unplanned > 0) and prompting firms to cut production.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inventory-Sign Inversion): When planned spending exceeds current output, goods sell faster than produced, depleting inventories (I_unplanned < 0) rather than accumulating them.

options_template.text: The economy is permanently stuck below Y* because firms have no inventory signal to change output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Missing Adjustment Mechanism): Negative unplanned inventory investment provides a direct quantity signal for firms to increase factory orders and output.

questions.title: Interpreting Output Above Equilibrium (Y > Y*)
questions.prompt_template: On the Keynesian cross diagram, suppose current real GDP (Y) lies to the right of the equilibrium intersection E* (so Y > Y*). How do inventories and firm production respond?

hints.text: Compare the height of the 45-degree line (Y) to the height of AE_planned to the right of E*.
Evaluate I_unplanned = Y - AE_planned when Y > AE_planned and trace how firms react to bloated warehouse stocks.

options_template.text: Planned expenditure exceeds output, depleting inventories and causing firms to expand production further away from Y*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Region Reversal Error): To the right of E*, the 45-degree line lies above the AE_planned line, meaning Y > AE_planned.

options_template.text: Output exceeds planned expenditure, causing unplanned inventory accumulation (I_unplanned > 0) and prompting firms to cut orders and reduce output toward Y*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. To the right of E*, Y > AE_planned, so unsold goods pile up in warehouses (I_unplanned > 0). Firms respond by slashing production and laying off workers until output falls back to Y*.

options_template.text: Output equals planned expenditure, so unplanned inventories remain zero and output stays at Y.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equilibrium Misidentification): Y = AE_planned holds only at E*, not to the right of it.

options_template.text: Unplanned inventories fall to negative values, forcing the government to raise lump-sum taxes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign and Policy Confusion): When Y > AE_planned, unplanned inventories are positive, and private firms—not tax hikes—drive the contraction back to Y*.

questions.topic: Multiplier Shifts in the Keynesian Cross
questions.title: Vertical Shift vs. Horizontal Output Change from Delta G > 0
questions.prompt_template: In the Keynesian cross diagram, an autonomous increase in government purchases (Delta G > 0) shifts the AE_planned line vertically upward. How does the resulting horizontal increase in equilibrium output (Delta Y*) compare to the vertical shift (Delta G)?

hints.text: Recall Figure 3 where a vertical shift of +20 moved equilibrium from Y_1* = 1,300 to Y_2* = 1,400.
Because the AE_planned line is upward-sloping (c > 0), moving right to catch up to the 45-degree line generates additional induced spending.

options_template.text: Delta Y* equals Delta G exactly because the equilibrium moves along a 45-degree line.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Induced Consumption): Moving along the 45-degree line means Delta AE = Delta Y*, where Delta AE includes both the vertical shift Delta G and induced consumption c Delta Y*.

options_template.text: Delta Y* is smaller than Delta G because the slope of AE_planned is less than 1.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverting the Multiplier): Because 0 < c < 1, the multiplier 1/(1 - c) is strictly greater than 1, making Delta Y* larger—not smaller—than Delta G.

options_template.text: Delta Y* is larger than Delta G by a factor of k_G = 1/(1 - c), because the upward shift triggers induced consumption along the flatter AE_planned line.
options_template.feedback: Correct. As illustrated in Figure 3, a vertical shift of Delta G = +20 moves the intersection with the 45-degree line horizontally by Delta Y* = k_G x Delta G = +100 (when c = 0.8).

options_template.text: Delta Y* is zero because the AE_planned line rotates clockwise around the original equilibrium E_1*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift vs. Rotation Error): An autonomous increase in G shifts AE_planned vertically upward in parallel; it does not rotate around E_1*.

questions.topic: Multiplier Shifts in the Keynesian Cross
questions.title: Graphical Shift from a Lump-Sum Tax Cut
questions.prompt_template: In the baseline Keynesian cross with lump-sum taxes, how does a $20 billion lump-sum tax cut (Delta T = -$20 billion) shift the AE_planned = (C_0 - cT + I_planned + G + NX) + cY line?

hints.text: Examine the autonomous expenditure intercept A_0 = C_0 - cT + I_planned + G + NX.
Compute Delta A_0 when Delta T = -$20 billion while holding C_0, I_planned, G, NX, and c constant.

options_template.text: It shifts the AE_planned line vertically upward by exactly $20 billion, identical to a $20 billion increase in G.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Full-Spending Tax Fallacy): Households save MPS of the tax cut in Round 1, so the vertical intercept rises by only c x $20 billion, not the full $20 billion.

options_template.text: It shifts the AE_planned line vertically upward by c x $20 billion (less than $20 billion) without changing its slope.
options_template.feedback: Correct. In A_0 = C_0 - cT + I_planned + G + NX, reducing T by $20 billion raises the vertical intercept by -c(-20) = +20c, shifting AE_planned upward in parallel by less than $20 billion.

options_template.text: It rotates the AE_planned line steeper from the same vertical intercept because lump-sum taxes affect the marginal tax rate t.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Lump-Sum vs. Proportional Tax Confusion): Lump-sum taxes T appear only in the intercept A_0, not in the slope c.

options_template.text: It shifts the AE_planned line vertically downward by c x $20 billion because lower tax revenue reduces government spending.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Balanced-Budget Assumption Error): Holding G constant, a tax cut raises disposable income and consumption, shifting AE_planned upward rather than downward.

questions.topic: Multiplier Shifts in the Keynesian Cross
questions.title: Graphical Effect of a Drop in Planned Investment
questions.prompt_template: Suppose business pessimism causes planned investment spending (I_planned) to fall autonomously while c, T, G, and NX remain unchanged. How does this appear on the Keynesian cross diagram?

hints.text: Determine whether I_planned affects the intercept A_0 or the slope c of AE_planned = A_0 + cY.
Trace the new intersection of a parallel-shifted AE_planned line with the fixed 45-degree line.

options_template.text: The AE_planned line shifts vertically downward in parallel, moving short-run equilibrium down and to the left along the 45-degree line.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A decline in I_planned lowers the vertical intercept A_0 without altering the slope c, shifting AE_planned downward in parallel and reducing Y* by a multiple of the drop.

options_template.text: The economy moves downward along the original AE_planned line without any shift of the curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement vs. Shift Error): Planned investment is an autonomous component of the vertical intercept A_0, so a change in I_planned shifts the entire curve.

options_template.text: The AE_planned line pivots flatter around its vertical intercept because lower investment reduces the MPC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Intercept Confusion): Changing I_planned changes the intercept A_0, not the household MPC (the slope).

options_template.text: The 45-degree line shifts downward while the AE_planned line stays fixed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (45-Degree Line Shift Fallacy): The 45-degree reference line (AE = Y) is a fixed geometric identity and never shifts.

questions.title: How a Higher MPC Changes the Keynesian Cross
questions.prompt_template: Comparing two closed economies with lump-sum taxes, Economy A has a higher marginal propensity to consume (MPC = 0.85) than Economy B (MPC = 0.60). Graphically, how does Economy A's AE_planned line compare to Economy B's?

hints.text: Connect the slope of AE_planned = A_0 + cY directly to the value of MPC.
Visualize how much farther right a steeper line must travel to intersect the 45-degree line after a vertical upward shift.

options_template.text: Economy A has a flatter AE_planned line, so a given vertical shift in autonomous spending produces a smaller horizontal change in Y*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-MPC Inversion): The slope of AE_planned equals MPC, so a higher MPC creates a steeper—not flatter—expenditure line.

options_template.text: Economy A has a steeper AE_planned line closer to the 45-degree line, so a given vertical shift in autonomous spending produces a larger horizontal change in Y*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A higher MPC steepens the AE_planned line toward the 45-degree line, increasing k_G = 1/(1 - MPC) so any vertical shift causes a larger horizontal shift in equilibrium output.

options_template.text: Both economies have the same slope of 1.0, differing only in their vertical intercepts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (45-Degree Slope Confusion): Only the 45-degree reference line has slope 1.0; AE_planned has slope equal to MPC < 1.

options_template.text: Economy A's AE_planned line slopes downward, causing autonomous spending increases to reduce Y*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative Slope Error): Since 0 < MPC < 1, AE_planned always slopes upward.

questions.title: How Proportional Taxes and Imports Alter the AE_planned Line
questions.prompt_template: Adding proportional income taxes (t > 0) and induced imports (m > 0) to the baseline Keynesian cross causes what graphical change to the AE_planned line?

hints.text: Compare the slope of the baseline line (c) with the open-economy tax-damped slope c(1 - t) - m.
Recall Figure 4: a flatter AE_planned curve means a smaller horizontal output change for any given vertical shift.

options_template.text: It steepens the AE_planned line from slope c to slope c(1 + t) + m, increasing the multiplier.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Leakage Direction Error): Taxes and imports siphon spending out of each round, reducing—not increasing—the slope of AE_planned.

options_template.text: It shifts the AE_planned line downward in parallel while keeping the slope unchanged at c.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Lump-Sum vs. Proportional Confusion): Only autonomous changes (like T_0 or IM_0) cause pure parallel shifts; proportional rates t and m change the slope.

options_template.text: It flattens the AE_planned line from slope c to slope c(1 - t) - m, shrinking the expenditure multiplier.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because every additional dollar of Y now generates only c(1 - t) - m in induced domestic spending, the AE_planned line becomes flatter and the multiplier drops to 1 / [1 - c(1 - t) + m].

options_template.text: It makes the 45-degree line flatter so that equilibrium output rises faster after any shock.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (45-Degree Line Distortion): The 45-degree line always has slope 1; leakages flatten the AE_planned schedule, not the 45-degree line.

questions.title: Graphical Effect of a Balanced-Budget Expansion
questions.prompt_template: On the baseline Keynesian cross diagram, how does a balanced-budget expansion (Delta G = Delta T = +$20 billion, with c = 0.8) shift the AE_planned line?

hints.text: Compute the net change in the vertical intercept A_0 = C_0 - cT + I_planned + G + NX when Delta G = Delta T = +20.
Once you find Delta A_0 = (1 - c)Delta G, multiply it by k_G = 1/(1 - c) to see how far Y* moves horizontally.

options_template.text: The AE_planned line does not shift at all because +Delta G and +Delta T cancel out at the vertical intercept.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equal-Intercept Cancellation Fallacy): Raising G shifts the intercept up by +20, while raising T shifts it down by only -0.8(20) = -16, leaving a net upward shift of +4.

options_template.text: The AE_planned line shifts vertically upward by (1 - c)Delta G = +$4 billion, which multiplies by k_G = 5 to raise Y* by exactly +$20 billion.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The net vertical intercept change is Delta A_0 = Delta G - c Delta T = (1 - 0.8)(20) = +$4 billion; multiplying +$4 billion by k_G = 5 yields Delta Y* = +$20 billion.

options_template.text: The AE_planned line shifts vertically upward by the full +$20 billion, raising Y* by +$100 billion.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Tax Offset): Financing the spending with a +$20 billion tax hike reduces Round 1 consumption by $16 billion, so the net vertical shift is +$4 billion, not +$20 billion.

options_template.text: The AE_planned line shifts vertically downward by -$4 billion, lowering Y* by -$20 billion.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal Error): Because Delta G enters at 100% while Delta T reduces consumption by only c < 100%, the net intercept shift is positive.

questions.title: Comparing Simple vs. Damped AE_planned Curves After an Autonomous Shock
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a simple closed-economy AE line (slope 0.8, k = 5) and a flatter leakage-damped AE line (slope 0.5, k = 2) initially intersect the 45-degree line at the exact same equilibrium E_1* (Y_1*). If both economies experience the exact same autonomous increase in government purchases (+Delta G), what does the diagram show?

hints.text: Recall Figure 4 comparing the simple AE line (k = 5) and the damped AE line (k = 2) starting from the same E_1*.
Multiply the identical vertical shift +Delta G by each curve's respective multiplier (5 vs. 2).

options_template.text: Both economies reach the exact same new equilibrium Y_2* because they experienced the same vertical shift +Delta G.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Blind Shift Error): Equal vertical shifts produce different horizontal changes in Y* whenever the two curves have different slopes.

options_template.text: The flatter leakage-damped AE line intersects the 45-degree line at a lower new equilibrium output (Y_2,damped*) than the steeper simple AE line.
options_template.feedback: Correct. As shown in Figure 4, because the damped AE line is flatter (slope 0.5 vs. 0.8), the same vertical shift +Delta G produces a smaller horizontal expansion (k = 2 vs. k = 5).

options_template.text: The flatter leakage-damped AE line intersects the 45-degree line at a higher new equilibrium output because its vertical intercept started higher.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept vs. Multiplier Confusion): The size of Delta Y* depends on the slope (multiplier) and the shift +Delta G, not on the initial intercept level.

options_template.text: Equilibrium output falls in the damped economy because tax and import leakages exceed 100% of +Delta G.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative-Multiplier Fallacy): As long as the domestic slope c(1 - t) - m is positive (0.5 here), the multiplier is still greater than 1 (k = 2 > 1), so Y* rises.

questions.title: Calculating Break-Even Disposable Income
questions.prompt_template: Suppose aggregate autonomous consumption is C_0 = $120 billion and the marginal propensity to consume is MPC = 0.75. What is the break-even level of disposable income (Y_D) where private saving equals zero (S_private = 0)?

hints.text: At the break-even level of disposable income, consumption equals disposable income (C = Y_D), so S_private = 0.
Set Y_D = 120 + 0.75Y_D, collect the Y_D terms on the left side (0.25Y_D = 120), and solve for Y_D.

options_template.text: $160 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dividing by MPC Instead of MPS): Computing 120 / 0.75 = $160 billion divides by MPC rather than MPS = 1 - MPC = 0.25.

options_template.text: $480 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting C = Y_D gives Y_D = 120 + 0.75Y_D, so 0.25Y_D = 120 and Y_D = 120 / 0.25 = $480 billion.

options_template.text: $90 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplying C_0 by MPC): Computing 120 x 0.75 = $90 billion gives neither break-even income nor saving.

options_template.text: $150 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Adding MPS Fraction to C_0): Computing 120 x 1.25 = $150 billion ignores that 0.25Y_D must equal 120.

questions.title: Evaluating Private Saving at a Given Disposable Income
questions.prompt_template: An economy has an aggregate consumption function C = 150 + 0.80Y_D (in billions of dollars). If disposable income is Y_D = $1,000 billion, what is private saving (S_private)?

hints.text: Use either S_private = Y_D - C or the saving function S_private = -C_0 + (1 - c)Y_D.
First compute C = 150 + 0.80(1,000) = 950, then subtract C from Y_D = 1,000.

options_template.text: $350 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Sign on Autonomous Saving): Using +150 + 0.20(1,000) = $350 billion forgets that the saving function intercept is -C_0 = -$150 billion, not +$150 billion.

options_template.text: $200 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitting Autonomous Consumption): Computing 0.20(1,000) = $200 billion ignores the -$150 billion autonomous dis-saving intercept.

options_template.text: $950 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reporting Consumption Instead of Saving): C = 150 + 0.80(1,000) = $950 billion is aggregate consumption, not private saving.

options_template.text: $50 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Consumption is C = 150 + 0.80(1,000) = $950 billion, so S_private = Y_D - C = 1,000 - 950 = $50 billion (equivalently, -150 + 0.20 x 1,000 = $50 billion).

questions.title: Calculating Autonomous Aggregate Expenditure (A_0)
questions.prompt_template: A closed economy (NX = 0) has the following parameters (in billions of dollars): C_0 = 140, MPC = 0.75, lump-sum taxes T = 80, planned investment I_planned = 160, and government purchases G = 100. What is autonomous aggregate expenditure (A_0)?

hints.text: Substitute Y_D = Y - T into C = C_0 + cY_D before grouping all constant (non-Y) terms into A_0.
Recall A_0 = C_0 - cT + I_planned + G + NX, and be sure to multiply T = 80 by c = 0.75.

options_template.text: $340 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Autonomous expenditure is A_0 = C_0 - cT + I_planned + G = 140 - 0.75(80) + 160 + 100 = 140 - 60 + 260 = $340 billion.

options_template.text: $320 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Subtracting Full T Instead of cT): Computing 140 - 80 + 160 + 100 = $320 billion forgets to multiply lump-sum taxes T by the MPC (0.75).

options_template.text: $460 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Adding cT Instead of Subtracting): Computing 140 + 60 + 160 + 100 = $460 billion reverses the sign on taxes, treating taxes as an injection rather than a reduction in disposable income.

options_template.text: $400 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitting Lump-Sum Taxes): Computing 140 + 160 + 100 = $400 billion omits the -cT = -$60 billion tax term from the consumption function.

questions.title: Solving for Short-Run Equilibrium Output from AE_planned
questions.prompt_template: Suppose planned aggregate expenditure is given by AE_planned = 300 + 0.75Y (in billions of dollars). What is short-run equilibrium real GDP (Y*)?

hints.text: In short-run equilibrium, actual output equals planned aggregate expenditure: Y* = AE_planned.
Set Y* = 300 + 0.75Y*, subtract 0.75Y* from both sides to get 0.25Y* = 300, and divide by 0.25.

options_template.text: $400 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dividing by MPC Instead of 1 - MPC): Computing 300 / 0.75 = $400 billion divides autonomous spending by c rather than (1 - c).

options_template.text: $525 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Round Approximation): Computing 300 + 0.75(300) = $525 billion stops after only one round of induced consumption instead of solving Y* = AE_planned.

options_template.text: $1,200 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting Y* = 300 + 0.75Y* gives 0.25Y* = 300, so Y* = 300 / 0.25 = $1,200 billion.

options_template.text: $225 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplying A_0 by MPC): Computing 300 x 0.75 = $225 billion shrinks autonomous spending instead of multiplying it by k = 1/(1 - 0.75) = 4.

questions.title: Full Closed-Economy Equilibrium Output Calculation
questions.prompt_template: Consider a closed economy (NX = 0) with C = 100 + 0.80(Y - T), lump-sum taxes T = $100 billion, planned investment I_planned = $150 billion, and government purchases G = $130 billion. What is short-run equilibrium real GDP (Y*)?

hints.text: First simplify AE_planned = C + I_planned + G into the form A_0 + 0.80Y.

options_template.text: $1,400 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Subtracting Full T from A_0): Using A_0 = 100 - 100 + 150 + 130 = 280 gives 280 / 0.20 = $1,400 billion, forgetting to multiply T by c = 0.80.

options_template.text: $1,500 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Autonomous expenditure is A_0 = 100 - 0.80(100) + 150 + 130 = $300 billion. With k_G = 1/(1 - 0.80) = 5, equilibrium output is Y* = 5 x 300 = $1,500 billion.

options_template.text: $1,900 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitting Lump-Sum Taxes): Using A_0 = 100 + 150 + 130 = 380 gives 380 / 0.20 = $1,900 billion, ignoring the -$80 billion tax effect on consumption.

options_template.text: $375 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dividing A_0 by MPC): Computing 300 / 0.80 = $375 billion divides autonomous spending by c instead of (1 - c) = 0.20.

questions.title: Calculating Unplanned Inventory Investment
questions.prompt_template: In an economy where AE_planned = 260 + 0.80Y (in billions of dollars), firms currently produce real GDP of Y = $1,500 billion. What is unplanned inventory investment (I_unplanned), and how will firms respond?

hints.text: Evaluate AE_planned directly at Y = $1,500 billion before comparing it to actual output.
Use I_unplanned = Y - AE_planned: positive values mean unplanned accumulation (output cuts), while negative values mean depletion (output expansion).

options_template.text: I_unplanned = -$40 billion (unplanned depletion); firms will expand production.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal Error): Computing AE_planned - Y = 1,460 - 1,500 = -$40 billion reverses the identity I_unplanned = Y - AE_planned.

options_template.text: I_unplanned = +$200 billion (unplanned accumulation); firms will cut production.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Using Y - Y* Instead of Y - AE_planned): Comparing Y = 1,500 to equilibrium Y* = 1,300 gives +$200 billion, ignoring that induced consumption rises when Y = 1,500.

options_template.text: I_unplanned = +$40 billion (unplanned accumulation); firms will cut production.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At Y = 1,500, AE_planned = 260 + 0.80(1,500) = $1,460 billion. Thus I_unplanned = Y - AE_planned = 1,500 - 1,460 = +$40 billion, so unsold goods pile up and firms cut output.

options_template.text: I_unplanned = -$200 billion (unplanned depletion); firms will expand production.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Gap from Y*): Computing Y* - Y = 1,300 - 1,500 = -$200 billion both reverses the sign and ignores induced spending at Y = 1,500.

questions.title: Calculating Delta Y* from an Increase in Government Purchases
questions.prompt_template: In a closed economy with lump-sum taxes, the marginal propensity to save is MPS = 0.25. If government purchases increase by Delta G = +$35 billion, by how much does short-run equilibrium real GDP change (Delta Y*)?

hints.text: Recall that k_G = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / MPS.
Compute k_G = 1 / 0.25 = 4, then multiply k_G by Delta G = +$35 billion.

options_template.text: +$140 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. The autonomous spending multiplier is k_G = 1 / MPS = 1 / 0.25 = 4.0, so Delta Y* = 4.0 x (+$35 billion) = +$140 billion.

options_template.text: +$105 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Using the Tax Multiplier Formula): Multiplying by MPC / MPS = 0.75 / 0.25 = 3.0 gives +$105 billion, which applies to a lump-sum tax cut rather than direct government purchases.

options_template.text: +$35 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitting Induced Rounds): Assuming Delta Y* = Delta G ignores the multiplier rounds (or confuses an unfinanced spending hike with a balanced-budget expansion).

options_template.text: +$26.25 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplying by MPC): Computing 0.75 x $35 billion = $26.25 billion gives only the Round 2 induced consumption rather than total Delta Y*.

questions.title: Calculating Delta Y* from a Lump-Sum Tax Cut
questions.prompt_template: In a closed economy with lump-sum taxes and MPC = 0.80, Congress enacts a lump-sum tax cut of Delta T = -$25 billion (holding government purchases constant). By how much does short-run equilibrium real GDP change (Delta Y*)?

hints.text: Use the lump-sum tax multiplier formula k_T = -c / (1 - c).
Compute k_T = -0.80 / 0.20 = -4.0, then multiply by Delta T = -$25 billion (watching the double negative).

options_template.text: +$125 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Using k_G Instead of k_T): Multiplying $25 billion by k_G = 5 gives +$125 billion, forgetting that households save 20% of the tax cut in Round 1.

options_template.text: +$100 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. The lump-sum tax multiplier is k_T = -MPC / (1 - MPC) = -0.80 / 0.20 = -4.0, so Delta Y* = (-4.0) x (-$25 billion) = +$100 billion.

options_template.text: +$25 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unit-Multiplier Fallacy): Assuming Delta Y* = -Delta T ignores the induced consumption rounds triggered by the tax cut.

options_template.text: +$20 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stopping at Round 1): Computing -0.80 x (-$25 billion) = +$20 billion captures only the Round 1 increase in consumption, omitting all subsequent multiplier rounds.

questions.title: Sizing a Lump-Sum Tax Cut to Close an Output Gap
questions.prompt_template: A closed economy with lump-sum taxes and MPC = 0.80 is currently in short-run equilibrium at Y* = $1,800 billion, while potential GDP is $2,000 billion. Holding government purchases constant, what change in lump-sum taxes (Delta T) is required to close the $200 billion output gap?

hints.text: First determine the target change in equilibrium output: Delta Y* = $2,000B - $1,800B = +$200B.
Solve Delta Y* = k_T x Delta T for Delta T using k_T = -0.80 / (1 - 0.80) = -4.0.

options_template.text: Delta T = -$40 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dividing by k_G Instead of |k_T|): Dividing $200 billion by k_G = 5 gives -$40 billion, which is the required increase in G—not the required cut in lump-sum taxes.

options_template.text: Delta T = -$200 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring the Multiplier): Cutting taxes by the entire $200 billion gap would raise Y* by $800 billion, severely overshooting potential GDP.

options_template.text: Delta T = -$160 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplying Gap by MPC): Computing -0.80 x $200 billion = -$160 billion confuses the tax multiplier with the MPC.

options_template.text: Delta T = -$50 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. With MPC = 0.80, the lump-sum tax multiplier is k_T = -0.80 / 0.20 = -4.0. To achieve Delta Y* = +$200 billion, policymakers need Delta T = 200 / (-4.0) = -$50 billion.

questions.title: Calculating Delta Y* Under a Balanced-Budget Expansion
questions.prompt_template: In a closed economy with lump-sum taxes and MPC = 0.75, the government increases purchases by Delta G = +$45 billion and simultaneously raises lump-sum taxes by Delta T = +$45 billion. What is the net change in short-run equilibrium real GDP (Delta Y*)?

hints.text: Compute the output impact of Delta G and Delta T separately, then sum them.
Use k_G = 1 / 0.25 = 4.0 and k_T = -0.75 / 0.25 = -3.0 in Delta Y* = k_G Delta G + k_T Delta T.

options_template.text: $0 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Effect Balanced Budget Fallacy): Assuming spending and tax hikes cancel completely ignores that k_G = 4.0 exceeds |k_T| = 3.0.

options_template.text: +$180 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitting the Tax Contraction): Computing 4.0 x $45 billion = +$180 billion counts only the expansion from Delta G while ignoring the -$135 billion contraction from Delta T.

options_template.text: +$135 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Applying |k_T| Alone): Computing 3.0 x $45 billion = +$135 billion gives only the magnitude of the tax drag rather than the net effect of both policies.

options_template.text: +$45 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. With k_G = 4.0 and k_T = -3.0, Delta Y* = 4.0(45) + (-3.0)(45) = 180 - 135 = +$45 billion, confirming the balanced-budget multiplier k_BB = 1.0.

questions.title: Calculating Delta Y* with Proportional Taxes and Imports
questions.prompt_template: An open economy has marginal propensity to consume c = 0.80, marginal income tax rate t = 0.10, and marginal propensity to import m = 0.12. If autonomous exports rise by Delta EX_0 = +$40 billion, by how much does short-run equilibrium real GDP rise (Delta Y*)?

hints.text: First find the domestic marginal propensity to spend: slope = c(1 - t) - m.
Compute k_damped = 1 / [1 - (c(1 - t) - m)], then multiply by Delta EX_0 = +$40 billion.

options_template.text: +$200 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Tax and Import Leakages): Using the closed-economy lump-sum multiplier k = 1/(1 - 0.80) = 5.0 gives 5.0 x $40 billion = +$200 billion, omitting t and m.

options_template.text: +$100 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. The domestic marginal propensity to spend is c(1 - t) - m = 0.80(0.90) - 0.12 = 0.72 - 0.12 = 0.60. Thus k_damped = 1 / (1 - 0.60) = 2.5, and Delta Y* = 2.5 x $40 billion = +$100 billion.

options_template.text: +$50 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dividing by c Instead of 1 - slope): Computing (1 / 0.80) x $40 billion = +$50 billion misapplies the denominator of the leakage-damped multiplier.

options_template.text: +$40 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unit-Multiplier Fallacy): Assuming Delta Y* = Delta EX_0 ignores all induced domestic consumption rounds.

questions.title: Cumulative Output Increase Across the First Three Rounds
questions.prompt_template: In a closed economy with lump-sum taxes and MPC = 0.80, firms increase planned investment autonomously by Delta I_planned = +$50 billion. What is the cumulative increase in real GDP after the first THREE rounds of spending (Round 1 + Round 2 + Round 3)?

hints.text: Calculate the income generated in Round 1, Round 2, and Round 3 individually using MPC = 0.80.
Sum Delta Y_1 = 50, Delta Y_2 = 0.80(50) = 40, and Delta Y_3 = 0.80(40) = 32.

options_template.text: $32 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reporting Only Round 3): $32 billion (0.80^2 x 50) is solely the third-round addition to income, not the cumulative sum of the first three rounds.

options_template.text: $250 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reporting Infinite-Round Total): $250 billion (5 x 50) is the total long-run equilibrium change across infinite rounds, not the cumulative total after three rounds.

options_template.text: $122 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Round 1 adds $50 billion, Round 2 adds 0.80($50B) = $40 billion, and Round 3 adds 0.80($40B) = $32 billion, for a three-round cumulative increase of 50 + 40 + 32 = $122 billion.

options_template.text: $150 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Saving Leakages Across Rounds): Multiplying $50 billion by 3 assumes households spend 100% (MPC = 1) in each round rather than 80%.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Direct Infrastructure Spending vs. One-Time Tax Rebates
questions.prompt_template: When evaluating the 2009 American Recovery and Reinvestment Act and 2020–2021 fiscal relief packages, why did Congressional Budget Office (CBO) economists assign a higher short-run output multiplier to direct federal infrastructure purchases than to one-time lump-sum tax rebates?

hints.text: Compare the Round 1 spending impact of Delta G versus Delta T < 0 in the Keynesian cross.
Think about what households actually did with a substantial portion of one-time rebates—saving them or paying down credit card balances.

options_template.text: Direct purchases enter aggregate expenditure immediately at 100% of their dollar value, whereas households save part of one-time rebates or use them to pay down debt rather than spending every dollar immediately.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Direct government purchases (Delta G) inject 100% of each dollar into Round 1 demand, while lump-sum rebates (Delta T < 0) leak partially into household saving and debt repayment in Round 1.

options_template.text: One-time tax rebates reduce household disposable income, whereas infrastructure purchases increase disposable income directly.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Rebate Sign Error): Tax rebates increase—not reduce—household disposable income, but households do not spend 100% of that extra income immediately.

options_template.text: Infrastructure purchases permanently eliminate import leakages and proportional income taxes from the economy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Leakage-Elimination Myth): Both infrastructure purchases and tax rebates face subsequent tax and import leakages in later spending rounds; the key difference is the Round 1 leakage.

options_template.text: The balanced-budget multiplier proves that tax cuts always have a multiplier of zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Tax-Multiplier Fallacy): Lump-sum tax cuts have a positive expansionary impact (k_T < 0 with Delta T < 0); their multiplier is smaller than k_G, not zero.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Interpreting the 2020–2024 Pandemic Saving Surge and Drawdown
questions.prompt_template: BEA data tracked in FRED show that U.S. real disposable personal income (DSPIC96) rose during 2020–2021 fiscal relief while the personal saving rate (PSAVERT) surged from roughly 7% in late 2019 to over 30% in April 2020, building over $2 trillion in excess savings. How does this episode refine the simple Keynesian consumption function?

hints.text: Connect the 2020–2021 lockdowns on in-person services to the subsequent 2022–2024 drawdown of excess savings.
Recall the BEA/FRED discussion in Section 2 linking DSPIC96, PSAVERT, and PCECC96.

options_template.text: It proves that the marginal propensity to consume is always negative during recessions.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative-MPC Fallacy): The surge in saving reflected temporary lockdown restrictions on in-person services rather than a permanently negative MPC.

options_template.text: It shows that temporary shocks—such as lockdowns restricting in-person services—can sharply raise short-run saving above normal behavioral trends, creating buffers that later support real consumption (PCECC96) even when interest rates rise.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Pandemic restrictions temporarily suppressed spending out of fiscal relief, elevating PSAVERT and building excess savings that households drew down in 2022–2024 to keep PCECC96 resilient.

options_template.text: It proves that disposable income has no effect on consumer spending in the United States.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overgeneralization Error): The consumption function remains stable in normal times; 2020–2021 illustrates how extraordinary supply/lockdown constraints temporarily shift saving behavior.

options_template.text: It demonstrates that excess household savings automatically reduce potential GDP in subsequent years.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Buffer vs. Potential-GDP Confusion): Drawing down excess savings supported aggregate consumption demand in 2022–2024 rather than lowering potential GDP.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Interpreting the 2022 Retail Inventory Overhang
questions.prompt_template: After 2021 supply-chain bottlenecks, major U.S. retailers over-ordered merchandise just as consumers rotated spending back toward travel and dining. By mid-2022, warehouse stocks surged (reflected in FRED series CBI, Change in Private Inventories), leading retailers to slash factory orders. Which Keynesian cross mechanism does this episode directly illustrate?

hints.text: Identify whether bloated warehouse stocks represent I_unplanned > 0 or I_unplanned < 0.
Trace the Keynesian cross adjustment law when Y > AE_planned: unsold stock accumulates and firms cut factory orders.

options_template.text: Negative unplanned inventory investment (I_unplanned < 0) causing firms to rapidly expand manufacturing output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal Error): Bloated warehouse stocks represent positive unplanned inventory accumulation (I_unplanned > 0), not depletion.

options_template.text: Positive unplanned inventory accumulation (I_unplanned > 0) when output exceeds planned goods demand, inducing firms to cut orders and temporarily drag down production until inventories normalize.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When merchandise supply exceeded rotated consumer demand, unplanned inventory accumulation (I_unplanned > 0) prompted retailers to discount stock and slash new orders, temporarily slowing manufacturing output.

options_template.text: The balanced-budget multiplier operating through higher retail sales taxes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Irrelevant Mechanism): The 2022 retail inventory overhang was a private demand-rotation and inventory-adjustment shock, not a balanced-budget fiscal change.

options_template.text: An upward shift of the 45-degree line caused by higher shipping costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (45-Degree Line Shift Fallacy): The 45-degree line is a fixed accounting reference (AE = Y) and never shifts.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Raw Changes in Realized GDP (GDPC1) Do Not Measure Fiscal Multipliers
questions.prompt_template: A student proposes estimating the U.S. government-purchases multiplier by simply dividing the quarterly change in FRED series GDPC1 (real GDP) by the quarterly change in federal spending. Why do empirical macroeconomists reject this naive calculation?

hints.text: Recall the distinction between realized output (Y = AE_planned + I_unplanned) and pure autonomous spending shifts.
Think about what else changes in the same quarter as federal budgets—inventories, interest rates, prices, and expectations—and how economists isolate causal effects.

options_template.text: Because GDPC1 measures nominal GDP without adjusting for inflation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Real vs. Nominal Misreading): GDPC1 is already real GDP in billions of chained 2017 dollars; the problem is identification, not price deflation.

options_template.text: Because GDPC1 measures realized output (AE_planned + I_unplanned) and reflects simultaneous swings in inventories, interest rates, prices, and expectations, requiring plausibly exogenous policy shocks to identify the causal multiplier.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Raw changes in GDPC1 confound planned spending shifts with unplanned inventory swings and concurrent monetary, price, and expectation changes, so economists use plausibly exogenous shocks like military procurement or state formula grants.

options_template.text: Because federal government purchases are excluded from GDPC1 in the National Income and Product Accounts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (NIPA Exclusion Myth): Government purchases of final goods and services (G) are directly included in real GDP (GDPC1).

options_template.text: Because the Keynesian multiplier is always a fixed universal constant equal to 5.0, making empirical estimation unnecessary.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Universal-Constant Fallacy): Multipliers are conditional on capacity, leakages, and monetary responses, not universal constants.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Evaluating Built-In Stabilizers During the 2008–2009 and 2020 Downturns
questions.prompt_template: During the 2008–2009 Great Recession and the 2020 COVID-19 downturn, federal tax receipts fell automatically while Unemployment Insurance outlays (FRED: W825RC1) rose immediately as layoffs occurred, offsetting roughly 15% to 25% of initial GDP shocks. What is the primary policy advantage of these mechanisms over discretionary stimulus bills?

hints.text: Focus on timing: how quickly do tax withholding and Unemployment Insurance respond compared to drafting and passing a new federal law?
Recall Section 5's empirical discussion of W825RC1 and TGDEF during 2008–2009 and 2020.

options_template.text: They increase the size of the autonomous spending multiplier so that every shock produces larger output swings.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stabilizer-Multiplier Direction Error): Automatic stabilizers flatten the AE_planned line and shrink the multiplier, moderating—not amplifying—output swings.

options_template.text: They cushion disposable income and aggregate demand immediately as contractions begin, avoiding the legislative delays required to pass discretionary fiscal packages.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Progressive income taxes, corporate taxes, and Unemployment Insurance respond automatically to falling income and rising layoffs, buffering demand without waiting for Congressional votes.

options_template.text: They guarantee that the federal government runs a budget surplus during every recession.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Budget-Surplus Fallacy): Because tax receipts drop and UI outlays rise during a downturn, automatic stabilizers widen—rather than eliminate—the cyclical budget deficit (reflected in TGDEF).

options_template.text: They eliminate all unplanned inventory accumulation in every sector of the economy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Elimination Fallacy): Automatic stabilizers cushion roughly 15% to 25% of initial GDP shocks; they dampen rather than completely eliminate business cycles.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: The Dual Effect of Higher Marginal Tax Rates and Trade Openness
questions.prompt_template: Country X has a higher marginal income tax rate (t) and a higher marginal propensity to import (m) than Country Y, while both have the same MPC. How does this structural difference create a macroeconomic policy trade-off for Country X?

hints.text: Ask how a smaller multiplier affects both a positive fiscal stimulus (+Delta G) and a negative private investment shock (-Delta I_planned).
A smaller multiplier dampens all autonomous shocks—both the ones policymakers want to amplify (stimulus) and the ones they want to cushion (recessions).

options_template.text: Country X enjoys a larger discretionary fiscal multiplier, but suffers larger output collapses when private investment drops.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Leakage Reversal): Higher t and m flatten AE_planned and shrink the multiplier, reducing both discretionary potency and private-shock volatility.

options_template.text: Country X experiences smaller discretionary fiscal multipliers when trying to stimulate its economy, but benefits from stronger automatic stabilization that dampens output drops when private spending falls.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A flatter AE_planned line (slope c(1 - t) - m) cuts both ways: it reduces the bang-for-the-buck of discretionary stimulus while automatically moderating cyclical downturns.

options_template.text: Country X has a larger balanced-budget multiplier, while Country Y has a negative autonomous spending multiplier.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplier-Sign Error): Neither country has a negative autonomous spending multiplier, and higher tax/import leakages do not increase the balanced-budget multiplier.

options_template.text: Country X's higher import propensity eliminates the need for monetary policy by fixing the price level permanently.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Level Fixing Myth): Induced imports dampen the expenditure multiplier but do not permanently fix the aggregate price level.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Multipliers Are Larger in Deep Recessions Than Near Full Employment
questions.prompt_template: Why do macroeconomists emphasize that the fiscal multiplier is 'conditional, not a universal constant'—typically larger during a deep recession with near-zero interest rates and smaller when the economy is near full employment?

hints.text: Compare what happens to prices and interest rates when fiscal stimulus hits an economy with high unemployment versus one with tight supply bottlenecks.
Recall the 'Clear It Up' box in Section 5 explaining why effective multipliers approach zero near full employment.

options_template.text: Because near full employment, households legally cannot spend their disposable income, pushing MPC to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Legal-Constraint Myth): Near full employment, households still have a positive MPC; the multiplier shrinks due to supply constraints, rising prices, and higher interest rates.

options_template.text: Because in a deep recession with idle capacity and near-zero interest rates, extra demand mainly raises real output with minimal inflation or crowding out; near full employment, supply bottlenecks, rising prices, and higher interest rates crowd out private spending.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When idle labor and factories are abundant and interest rates are near zero, fiscal stimulus expands real output strongly; near full capacity, inflation and interest-rate crowding out push the effective multiplier closer to zero.

options_template.text: Because in a deep recession, the government automatically sets the marginal income tax rate t equal to zero.
