options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Tax-Rate Myth): Marginal tax brackets remain in place during recessions; state dependence arises from idle capacity, price pressure, and interest-rate responses.

options_template.text: Because the Keynesian cross applies only when inflation exceeds 10% per year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (High-Inflation Misattribution): The fixed-price Keynesian cross is most accurate when prices are sticky and capacity is idle, not during high inflation.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: How Permanent-Income Smoothing Dampens Temporary Tax Rebates
questions.prompt_template: Suppose the government announces a strictly one-time temporary tax rebate that households know will not be repeated next year. If households smooth consumption based on their permanent (long-run expected) income rather than solely current income, how does this affect the short-run multiplier?

hints.text: Ask how a forward-looking household reacts to a one-time $1,000 bonus versus a permanent $1,000 annual raise.
Recall the third real-world multiplier dampener in Section 5: households smoothing consumption based on permanent income.

options_template.text: It amplifies the multiplier because households spend more than 100% of a temporary rebate immediately.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overspending Confusion): Consumption smoothers spread a temporary windfall over many future years rather than spending over 100% immediately.

options_template.text: It dampens the short-run multiplier because households save most of a temporary windfall to smooth consumption over time, lowering their effective short-run MPC out of temporary income.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When households base spending on permanent income, a one-time rebate barely changes lifetime resources, so they save most of it—shrinking Round 1 spending and dampening the multiplier.

options_template.text: It has no effect on the multiplier because the Keynesian cross assumes permanent income always equals current disposable income.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Model-Boundary Confusion): The simple Keynesian cross abstracts from permanent-income smoothing, which is precisely one of the three real-world dampeners discussed in Section 5.

options_template.text: It turns the autonomous spending multiplier negative because households cut spending whenever they receive a rebate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative-Response Fallacy): Households still spend a small positive fraction of a temporary rebate; the multiplier is dampened, not negative.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Synchronized Household Deleveraging During a Downturn
questions.prompt_template: Following a sharp decline in housing wealth during a sticky-price recession, millions of households simultaneously cut autonomous consumption (C_0) to rebuild personal savings and pay down debt. According to the Keynesian cross and the paradox of thrift, what macroeconomic outcome can result?

hints.text: Trace the effect of a drop in C_0 on AE_planned, equilibrium output Y*, and induced private saving S = -C_0 + sY_D.
Apply the paradox of thrift from Section 2 to a synchronized household deleveraging shock.

options_template.text: Aggregate expenditure falls, firms face unplanned inventory accumulation and cut production, and falling national income can leave total private saving unchanged or even lower than before.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Although each household intends to save more, the collective drop in C_0 shifts AE_planned downward, reducing equilibrium income Y and induced saving (sY_D) so aggregate saving may fail to rise.

options_template.text: Equilibrium real GDP rises automatically because lower consumption lowers the break-even income level.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Break-Even vs. Equilibrium Confusion): A lower break-even income reflects reduced autonomous consumption, which shifts AE_planned downward and contracts—not expands—equilibrium GDP.

options_template.text: Unplanned inventory depletion forces firms to hire more workers to replenish empty shelves.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inventory-Direction Reversal): Cutting autonomous consumption reduces planned spending below current output, causing unplanned inventory accumulation (I_unplanned > 0), not depletion.

options_template.text: The autonomous spending multiplier increases because households are saving a larger share of their income.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Saving-Multiplier Sign Error): Higher saving reduces rather than increases the spending multiplier.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Consequences of Equal Spending and Tax Cuts in a Recession
questions.prompt_template: During a recession, a state or national legislature bound by a strict balanced-budget rule reduces government purchases by $30 billion and simultaneously cuts lump-sum taxes by $30 billion (Delta G = Delta T = -$30 billion). In the baseline Keynesian cross, what is the macroeconomic impact of this 'budget-neutral' shrinkage?

hints.text: Apply Delta Y* = k_G Delta G + k_T Delta T when both Delta G and Delta T are negative and equal (-$30 billion).
Remember that k_BB = +1 works symmetrically in reverse: a balanced-budget contraction shrinks Y* by Delta G.

options_template.text: It is completely neutral (Delta Y* = 0) because the $30 billion tax cut fully offsets the $30 billion cut in government purchases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Symmetric Cancellation Fallacy): Because |k_G| > |k_T|, cutting G and T by identical amounts is not neutral; the direct spending cut outweighs the tax cut.

options_template.text: It is expansionary (Delta Y* = +$30 billion) because private households always spend tax cuts more efficiently than governments spend G.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal on Balanced-Budget Multiplier): Because households save MPS of the $30 billion tax cut while the $30 billion cut in G reduces demand by 100% immediately, net AE_planned falls.

options_template.text: It is contractionary, reducing short-run equilibrium real GDP by $30 billion (Delta Y* = -$30 billion) because k_BB = 1.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Applying the balanced-budget multiplier (k_BB = k_G + k_T = 1) to Delta G = Delta T = -$30 billion yields Delta Y* = 1 x (-$30 billion) = -$30 billion, deepening the recession.

options_template.text: It reduces equilibrium GDP by k_G x $30 billion because lump-sum tax cuts never stimulate household consumption.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Tax Cushion): The $30 billion tax cut does stimulate consumption by c x $30 billion in Round 1, partially—but not fully—offsetting the cut in G.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: How Import Leakages Create Cross-Border Stimulus Spillovers
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a small, highly open economy with a high marginal propensity to import (m = 0.30) enacts a large domestic fiscal stimulus (+Delta G). How does this high import propensity affect both domestic equilibrium GDP and its trading partners?

hints.text: Follow the dollars spent by domestic households on imported cars, electronics, or vacations during each round of the stimulus.
Remember that one country's induced imports (mY) are its trading partners' exports.

options_template.text: It increases the domestic multiplier above 1/(1 - c) while reducing trading partners' exports.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Import-Leakage Sign Reversal): A higher m reduces domestic induced spending c(1 - t) - m, shrinking the domestic multiplier while raising foreign exports.

options_template.text: It dampens the domestic multiplier because part of each income round leaks into foreign goods, while simultaneously boosting trading partners' autonomous exports and output.
options_template.feedback: Correct. High import leakages flatten the domestic AE_planned line (lowering domestic Delta Y*), while the induced import purchases become higher exports (EX_0) for trading partners.

options_template.text: It has no effect on the domestic multiplier because imports are counted as part of domestic planned investment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Net-Exports Accounting Error): Imports are subtracted from planned aggregate expenditure (NX = EX - IM), not added to domestic investment.

options_template.text: It forces the domestic economy's marginal income tax rate t to fall to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Trade Conflation): Trade openness (m) and the marginal income tax rate (t) are separate leakage parameters.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Interest-Rate Crowding Out and Price-Level Feedback Dampen the Multiplier
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an economy is approaching full capacity when the government enacts a large fiscal expansion (+Delta G). Beyond proportional taxes and imports, which two macroeconomic feedback channels cause the actual increase in real GDP to be smaller than the fixed-price Keynesian cross prediction?

hints.text: Recall the three real-world multiplier dampeners beyond tax and import leakages listed in Section 5.
Think about what happens to (1) the aggregate price level and (2) interest rates and private investment when nominal income rises near full capacity.

options_template.text: Falling aggregate prices erode nominal wages, and lower interest rates discourage household saving.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Reversal on Prices and Rates): A fiscal expansion near capacity pushes aggregate prices and interest rates upward, not downward.

options_template.text: Rising aggregate prices erode real purchasing power, and higher nominal income raises money demand and interest rates, partially crowding out interest-sensitive private investment.
options_template.feedback: Correct. As explained in Section 5, when fiscal stimulus pushes the economy toward capacity, rising prices and higher interest rates crowd out private spending, making the real-world multiplier smaller than the fixed-price benchmark.

options_template.text: Higher government purchases reduce autonomous exports directly and force the 45-degree line to shift downward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (45-Degree Line Shift Fallacy): The 45-degree line never shifts, and the key macroeconomic dampeners beyond tax/import leakages are price-level increases and interest-rate crowding out.

options_template.text: Higher output causes unplanned inventory accumulation to turn permanently negative, preventing firms from hiring.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inventory-Hiring Contradiction): Negative unplanned inventory investment signals firms to expand hiring and output, not stop hiring.
